title: Firefox PDF JavaScript execution is actually a feature
summary: Protect your app from PDF JavaScript injection (CVE-2024-4367 in Firefox). Explore PDF.js, sanitization methods, and understand Mozilla's sandboxing approach.
body_markdown:
During a recent penetration test, we found a vulnerability with PDF JavaScript execution in Firefox’s native PDF viewer. This specific vulnerability is known as[CVE-2024-4367](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2024-4367) and affects Firefox browser versions 126 and under.


The vulnerability involves users being able to inject JavaScript into a PDF that runs in the browser runtime.


## Context on Firefox’s PDF viewer


Firefox maintains PDF.js, a common tool that web applications can use to render PDFs directly in webpages, like with[React PDF Viewer](https://react-pdf-viewer.dev/) . They also use PDF.js to display PDFs that you may download across the internet, so you don’t have to download extra software just to view PDFs.


Our pentester linked a really great[resource that includes 11 vulnerable PDFs](https://github.com/luigigubello/PayloadsAllThePDFs/tree/main) . All the PDFs will basically try to inject JavaScript using various techniques from different CVEs. A few of them were used to find vulnerabilities in our own application, which could potentially cause code injection and compromise our users.


## Handling PDF vulnerabilities in your web app


React PDF viewer actually has some pretty sane defaults. All script execution is disabled by default. This has been circumvented in the past, so keeping your PDF web renderer up to date and using Dependabot to detect vulnerable versions you have installed is *crucial* .


An additional bonus step that I think everyone should take is to santizie PDFs. There are some paid services which claim to be the best, but there are also some free tools that work just fine for most use cases.


jsx


```text
mutool clean   -  f   -  g   -  s dirty  .  pdf sanitized  .  pdf
```


jsx


```text
gs   -  dSAFER   -  dNOPAUSE   -  dQUIET   -  dBATCH   -  sDEVICE  =  pdfwrite   -  dCompatibilityLevel  =  1.4   -  dOptimize  =  true   -  sOutputFile  =  sanitized  .  pdf dirty  .  pdf
```


jsx


```text
qpdf   --  qdf   --  object  -  streams  =  disable dirty  .  pdf sanitized  .  pdf
```


All three of these free tools will sanitize your PDFs. In practice, you just need to run these tools in your backend application, for example:


jsx


```text
// SanitizePDF takes a PDF file reader and returns a sanitized version using mutool clean.
// The function creates a temporary file for the input, runs mutool clean on it,
// and returns a reader for the sanitized output.
func SanitizePDF(inputReader io  .  Reader) (io  .  ReadCloser  ,   error)   {
// Create temporary files for input and output
tmpInput  ,   err   :  =   os  .  CreateTemp(  ""  ,   "  pdf_input_*.pdf  "  )
if   err   !=   nil   {
return   nil  ,   errors  .  Wrap(err  ,   "  failed to create temporary input file  "  )
}
defer os  .  Remove(tmpInput  .  Name())
defer tmpInput  .  Close()


tmpOutput  ,   err   :  =   os  .  CreateTemp(  ""  ,   "  pdf_output_*.pdf  "  )
if   err   !=   nil   {
return   nil  ,   errors  .  Wrap(err  ,   "  failed to create temporary output file  "  )
}
defer os  .  Remove(tmpOutput  .  Name())
defer tmpOutput  .  Close()


// Copy input to temporary file
if   _  ,   err   :  =   io  .  Copy(tmpInput  ,   inputReader)  ;   err   !=   nil   {
return   nil  ,   errors  .  Wrap(err  ,   "  failed to copy input to temporary file  "  )
}


// Run mutool clean
cmd   :  =   exec  .  Command(  "  mutool  "  ,   "  clean  "  ,   "  -f  "  ,   "  -g  "  ,   "  -s  "  ,   tmpInput  .  Name()  ,   tmpOutput  .  Name())
if   output  ,   err   :  =   cmd  .  CombinedOutput()  ;   err   !=   nil   {
return   nil  ,   errors  .  Wrapf(err  ,   "  mutool clean failed: %s  "  ,   string(output))
}


// Open the sanitized file for reading
sanitizedFile  ,   err   :  =   os  .  Open(tmpOutput  .  Name())
if   err   !=   nil   {
return   nil  ,   errors  .  Wrap(err  ,   "  failed to open sanitized file  "  )
}


return   sanitizedFile  ,   nil
}
```


Ideally, this is done before uploading your PDFs to your storage provider like AWS S3.


After implementing our mutools cleaner utility, I was still able to upload[payload1.pdf](https://github.com/luigigubello/PayloadsAllThePDFs/blob/main/pdf-payloads/payload1.pdf) from the repository I linked earlier, and to my surprise, the alert(1) was still executing. Here is the actual code of the PDF where the injection is happening


jsx


```text
3   0   obj
<<
/  Type   /  Action
/  S   /  JavaScript
/  JS (app  .  alert\(  1  \); Object  .  getPrototypeOf(  function*  (){}  )  .  constructor   =   null; ((  function*  (){}  )  .  constructor(  "  document.write('<script>confirm(document.cookie);</script><iframe src=https://14.rs>');  "  ))()  .  next();)
>>
endobj
```


This was quite a bit of a headache to figure out. Chrome did not display the alert, only Firefox. I wasn’t testing on a vulnerable version of Firefox. I tried about five different PDF sanitizer tools and none of them would sanitize this. I even opened an issue on[Mozilla’s PDF.js repository](https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/issues/19860) (which I closed shortly after I did more research).


## What does Mozilla say about JavaScript execution in PDF.js?


After a lot of Google searches and looking through GitHub issues and StackOverflow, I finally found a link to an article by Mozilla.


[Implementing form filling and accessibility in the Firefox PDF viewer](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2021/10/implementing-form-filling-and-accessibility-in-the-firefox-pdf-viewer/)


This article has a section about “ **Safely Executing JavaScript within PDFs** ” which can be paraphrased to read


> JavaScript in PDFs can be used for many things, but is most commonly used to validate data entered by the user or automatically calculate formulas. We settled on using a ComponentUtils.Sandbox for the Firefox built-in viewer. ComponentUtils.Sandbox has been used for years now in WebExtensions, so this implementation is battle tested and very safe.


This process basically involves the PDF viewer collecting fields that execute JS, copying them to a sandbox, and then executing them.


## What even is a Sandbox?


A sandbox is typically an execution runtime that is stripped from APIs that can call external services. In Firefox’s case, it removes[XHR](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest) ,[window](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window) , and[Components](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/xpcom/index.html) among others. This essentially cuts off access to network requests, accessing window objects in the webpage, and prevents access to Firefox’s built‐in JavaScript engine (SpiderMonkey).


## It’s a feature… not a bug


Sandboxing JavaScript is safe enough. I now needed to make sure that payload1.pdf was actually executing in a sandbox. We can update the payload like so


jsx


```text
3   0   obj
<<
/  Type   /  Action
/  S   /  JavaScript
/  JS (
var hasDOM     =   \(  typeof   window         !==   "  undefined  "  \);       // should be false
var hasXHR     =   \(  typeof   XMLHttpRequest   !==   "  undefined  "  \);    // false
var hasComp    =   \(  typeof   Components      !==   "  undefined  "  \);     // false
app  .  alert\(
"  window?   "     +   hasDOM    +   "  \\n  "   +
"  XHR?   "        +   hasXHR    +   "  \\n  "   +
"  Components?   "  +   hasComp
\);
/* --- now your original payload: --- */
app  .  alert\(  1  \);
Object  .  getPrototypeOf\(  function  \  *  \  (  \  )  \  {  \  }  \)\  .  constructor   =   null;
\(\(  function  \  *  \  (  \  )  \  {  \  }  \)\  .  constructor\(
"  document.write('<script>confirm(document.cookie);</script><iframe src=https://14.rs>');  "
\)\)\(\)\  .  next\(\);
)
>>
endobj
```


The payload essentially just looks like this:


jsx


```text
var   hasDOM     =   (  typeof   window         !==   "  undefined  "  )  ;    // should be false
var   hasXHR     =   (  typeof   XMLHttpRequest   !==   "  undefined  "  )  ;    // false
var   hasComp    =   (  typeof   Components      !==   "  undefined  "  )  ;    // false
app  .  alert(
"  window?   "     +   hasDOM    +   "  \n  "   +
"  XHR?   "        +   hasXHR    +   "  \n  "   +
"  Components?   "  +   hasComp
)  ;
```


After updating the payload, we can confirm the injection is actually running in sandboxed JS.


## Conclusion


This information can be very useful for both pentesters and web developers. Pentesters should be aware that the Firefox PDF viewer actually allows script execution. Chrome only allows a small subset of script execution through[their custom API](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/705d4e18b4130157210ee9e4a65ab364fa29758d/chrome/browser/resources/pdf/pdf_scripting_api.ts) , Safari does not allow JavaScript execution at all, and other browsers vary.


For pentesters, it may be exciting to see the alert pop up and you think you’ve found a vulnerability, but you should always check if the execution is sandboxed (see payload above) before you report an issue.


For web developers, it’s important to keep your dependencies up to date and have a service that sanitizes PDFs. It is your responsibility to keep your users safe.
